# Skills, graph and loop: the improvement plan (2026-11-06)

Why: features were added one regex and one special case at a time (43 routing tests in the controller, 28 in
local-skills, ~20 stages in one `handle()`), and nothing measures a feature on its own. A fix for one request can
break another, and the same mistake comes back. This plan turns the features into **skills** with a contract,
puts a **check that can fail** inside each one (the loop), wires them with explicit **nodes, edges and gates**
(the graph), and makes every accepted fix a **permanent constraint** checked by evals (the learning edge).

Goals that do not change (they are the acceptance test of every phase):

1. Local first: AFM, Decima, Copilot inline completion and Spotlight do as much as they can, at no cost.
2. Few frontier calls: Codex only through a gate, and with a redacted capsule (summaries, paths, line ranges), not
   raw documents. Measured per task: frontier calls, bytes sent.
3. Quality at Codex-alone level on the benchmark suites (code-eval, framework-eval).
4. Nothing that works today breaks: every phase ships behind a flag, runs in shadow first, and must pass the
   eval gate (no regression in any skill) plus `npm test`.

## 1. Skill packs (what exists today, grouped)

| pack | what it holds today | lane |
|---|---|---|
| `core` | triage, routing, final answer, citation/grounding checks, memory, escalation | contained |
| `files` | find files (name), folder overview, document questions, sheets, slides, action-item tables, MCP read_document/find_files | contained |
| `code` | small edits, local code jobs, codegen, Copilot S5 tier, afm_code, docstrings, error triage, rename | wide (branch) |
| `git` | git overview, GitHub status, change summary, commit message, release notes, job list/compare/apply, sessions | contained (apply: wide) |
| `writing` | LaTeX compile/refs/table/polish, afm_write, afm_summarize, translation | contained |
| `mac` | open app/terminal/editor, launch app, Mac health, command help, run command (approval) | contained |
| `security` | security check, privacy scan (the security gate itself stays in core code, not a skill) | contained |
| `web` | web search (approval), SearXNG / fallbacks | contained, egress |
| `frontier` | Codex hand-off (read-only answer, worktree session), Copilot chat hand-off | egress |

Each pack is a folder `skills/<id>/` with `skill.json` (the contract, §2), `evals/cases.jsonl` (public cases on
fixtures or this repository) and later `constraints.md` (the learning edge, §6). Code stays where it is; the
manifest points at it. Moving code is not part of this plan.

## 2. The skill contract (`skill.json`) and compatibility rules

Fields: `id`, `version` (semver), `contract` (manifest format version), `description`, `examples` (requests it
must take; used by the router in phase 3 and by evals), `reasonCodes` (the controller reason codes this skill
owns; exact or `prefix_*`), `capabilities` (`read`, `propose`, `job`, `run_approved`, `network`, `frontier`),
`lane` (`contained` | `wide` | `irreversible`), `egress` (`none` | `query` | `capsule`), `checks` (the GREEN
conditions its loop uses), `budget` (AFM calls, latency, frontier calls per request).

Rules the registry enforces (load fails in tests and in development; a third-party skill is skipped):

- ids unique; every reason code owned by exactly one skill; every reason code the controller emits is owned
  (a test scans the controller), so a new branch cannot ship without a skill.
- A manifest can only **narrow** what the security gate allows, never widen it. `irreversible` work (delete,
  push, send, migrate, credentials) has no automatic lane: it is not a high threshold, it is a closed lane.
- `frontier` capability implies `egress: capsule`; `network` implies `egress: query` or more. A skill that says
  `egress: none` and makes a network call fails its eval (the runner checks).
- `contract` major version must match the registry; new optional fields are added in minor versions only.
- Third-party skills (phase 6+, `~/OnBud/skills.d/`) are off by default, cannot declare `frontier`,
  `run_approved` or `irreversible`, and run with read + propose only.

## 3. The graph (between nodes)

Node kinds (from the referenced post, mapped to this system):

- **Splitter**: the router and the job planner. It decides which units exist; it is where the learning edge lands.
- **Worker**: one skill doing one unit with one lens, in its own context (AFM for text, Copilot for code,
  Codex as the worker of last resort).
- **Code node**: anything with one correct answer: Spotlight/mdfind queries, ranking, dedupe, merge, diff
  checks, test runs, language detection, redaction. Never a model call.
- **Gate**: decides what goes on. Reads evidence in this order: deterministic results → this run's trajectory →
  how often this node's work was rolled back → Decima's difficulty score → the model's own claim (last).

Edges only where a value crosses. Independent nodes run in parallel: e.g. name search ∥ content search ∥ Decima
scoring; reading three documents ∥. Every arrow in today's chain is checked with "does the next step read the
previous one's output?"; where it does not, the wait is removed (phase 4).

Tiers as nodes (cost order): code nodes (free) → AFM (free, on-device) → Copilot inline (free, code only) →
Decima (free, a score for the gate) → Codex (subscription, egress). Codex gets a unit only when the gate says
so, and gets the unit, not the whole conversation.

## 4. The loop (inside a node): produce → check → correct → repeat until green

The check is written first and is a program. Per pack:

| pack | GREEN (programmatic) | not a check |
|---|---|---|
| core | reply language = request language; every cited path exists; quoted lines are in the evidence | "looks fine" |
| files | each result exists, and its name/title/content matches the query's topic terms | model confidence |
| code | tests exit 0; the diff touches only the planned files; no stub left | "no error raised" |
| git | numbers/branches in the answer equal `git` output | |
| writing | latexmk exits 0; citation keys and \ref labels unchanged; markup tokens preserved | |
| mac | the app/window opened (exit code, window check) | |
| security | every finding has file:line and a masked value | |
| web | every claim carries a source URL that was fetched | |
| frontier | capsule passes redaction; frontier calls ≤ budget | |

A failed check returns the **unit, not the batch**, with four things: UNIT, VERDICT, REASON, EVIDENCE, and
SCOPE ("fix this file only"). At most three corrections; a unit failing three times goes back to the splitter
(the plan was wrong), or to the user.

## 5. Gates and lanes (blast radius, not confidence)

- **contained** (answers, proposals, read-only): opens first, automatic.
- **wide** (local jobs on their own branch, multi-file edits): deterministic checks + clean trajectory; the human
  approves once, at the merge ("반영"). Not at each step.
- **irreversible**: never automatic, whatever the score.
- **egress gate** (any frontier or web call): allowed only by policy + approval rules that exist today; the
  payload is the redacted capsule; the eval runner counts bytes sent.

## 6. Return paths

- **Correction edge** (short): the gate sends one unit back to its producer, with the scope line (§4).
- **Learning edge** (long): an accepted fix becomes a constraint in `skills/<id>/constraints.md`, which the
  splitter/worker reads ("folder names in the request are search scope, not search terms"). A constraint is
  accepted only with an eval case that fails without it and passes with it. Constraints are versioned like code.

## 7. The improvement loop (how fixes are made from now on)

1. A failure (user report or a red eval) becomes an eval case first: the request, the fixture, the GREEN checks.
   Personal cases (real paths, real documents) go to `~/OnBud/runtime/evals/private/` and are never committed.
2. The case is red on the current code (baseline).
3. One skill is changed, scope-limited to that skill (by hand or by Codex in a worktree with that scope).
4. `tools/skill-eval.ts` runs all skills: the case turns green and no other case turns red (the gate).
   `npm test`, framework-eval (s2/s3) and code-eval (S5) must not regress for changes to `core` or `code`.
5. Accepted: commit with the case; derive a constraint if the cause is general (learning edge).
6. The scorecard records the path, not only the answer: route, skill, AFM calls, frontier calls, bytes sent,
   latency. A cheaper path at the same score is an improvement too.

## 8. Where Shortcuts fit

- **Triggers (entry points)**: hotkey, Share Sheet ("Ask OnBud about this file"), Focus/time automations.
  They call the `afm` CLI or the controller's local API; no logic in the shortcut.
- **Tool nodes for macOS-only actions**: Calendar, Reminders, Notes, Mail drafts, Photos, Focus, Ghostty App
  Intents, via `shortcuts run <name>` as a code node. An allow-list in `skills/mac/shortcuts.json` names each
  shortcut, its input/output and its lane; sending, deleting or paying shortcuts are irreversible: closed lane.
- **Not**: the loop or graph engine (no versioning, diff or tests, slow, weak state and branching), and not
  calling Apple Intelligence models through Shortcuts as an API (the model notice forbids programmatic access
  through Apple software except as expressly permitted).
- Scheduled evals run from launchd (or a Personal Automation that calls the same script), not inside Shortcuts.

## 9. Security and distribution

- Manifests and cases in the repository contain no personal paths, names or documents; a test checks for `/Users/`
  and home-folder names. Private cases live in runtime/ (git-ignored, mode 700).
- Skills get capabilities, not code access: a manifest cannot enable network, frontier or writes the gate
  forbids; external skill folders are read + propose only.
- File and web contents are data, never instructions (unchanged); constraints are written only from accepted,
  eval-backed fixes, never from document text.
- The eval runner runs with `readOnly`, no frontier and `ONBUD_BENCH=1` (its log lines are marked and left out
  of calibration). It opens no apps and starts no jobs.

## 10. Phases (each: flag off by default → shadow → eval gate → on)

| phase | work | exit criteria |
|---|---|---|
| P0 (done 2026-11-06) | manifests for 9 packs, registry + coverage test, programmatic checks, `skill-eval.ts` (`--repeat`, `--baseline` gate), seed cases from known failures, baseline scorecard | npm test green; no behavior change |
| P1 (done 2026-11-06) | core contracts: reply-language contract (detect from request text without paths/quotes/identifiers; post-check on every answer; masked translation, original kept if a masked part is lost), `ONBUD_LANG_CONTRACT` on/shadow/off | reply-language family green; 0 regressions |
| P2 (done 2026-11-06) | files: find frame (names, topic, content cue; en/ko), name ∥ title ∥ content Spotlight search, merged ranking with "matched by", "which file mentions X" recognised, Unicode file names; generated public fixtures (`fixture:topic-docs`); `ONBUD_FIND_TOPIC=off` | find-by-topic family green (4 wordings); Sparse Attention fixed; 0 regressions |
| P3 | router: skill choice from manifests (AFM enum over descriptions + examples) in shadow next to the regex chain; switch per skill when they agree on evals and real logs | agreement ≥ 95% on cases; no regression |
| P4 | graph executor for multi-unit work: parallel independent nodes, unit return with scope, 3-attempt cap; first user: local jobs | job evals green, time ↓ |
| P5 | learning edge: constraints files, eval-backed | constraints have cases |
| P6 | Shortcuts tool nodes (allow-list) and triggers; third-party skills folder (read + propose) | mac cases green; closed lanes tested |

## 11. Baseline (P0, 2026-11-06, single runs, AFM on macOS 27.2)

9/17 green: code 1/1 · core 1/3 · files 2/5 · git 0/2 · mac 2/3 · security 1/1 · web 1/1 · writing 0/1.
The red cases are the work list, in plan order:

- core (P1): a Korean request answered in English (`core-ko-answer-ko`); a plain README summary escalated.
- files (P2): "about Sparse Attention in the content" searched the words "research, paper, about" by name; content
  search finds the paper. "Which file defines the routing thresholds?" answered `routes.py` (does not exist).
- git: "What is the current git branch?" escalated on the answer guardrail instead of reading `git branch`.
- mac (P3, router): "Check the health of my Mac." missed the Mac-health skill (the regex wants "mac … health").
- writing: "compile the LaTeX paper here" with no .tex file went to a generic answer that invented a path.

AFM's answers vary between runs (one case flipped between two runs): the gate uses `--repeat 3`.

## 12. Generality: skills that work on other people's Macs (added 2026-11-06)

A fix that only makes one of the author's requests pass ("find the Sparse Attention paper") is not accepted. Gate:

- **Public paraphrase families.** Each fix lands with ≥ 3 public cases of the same family (`"family"` in the
  case): two wordings, both languages (ko/en), on repository fixtures or generated fixtures, plus the private
  case that triggered it. A family must pass as a whole.
- **No new trigger regex without a family.** Routing words belong in the manifest's `examples` (P3 router), not
  in new regexes in the controller; a regex may stay only as a fast path that a family covers.
- **Environment profiles.** Skills declare `requires` (`apfel`, `spotlight`, `decima?`, `copilot?`, `searxng?`,
  `gh?`, an app); `?` means optional with a fallback. The eval runs in two profiles: full (this Mac) and minimal
  (Decima, Copilot, web and gh off; Spotlight index assumed). A skill must pass its minimal-profile cases.
- **Locale and apps.** No assumption about the user's language, terminal (Ghostty/iTerm/Terminal), editor or
  folder names; the user's choices come from `config/apps.json` or the system default (already the case for
  terminals and editors).

## 13. New and extended skills (common Mac work)

Usage surveys (Setapp Mac Apps Reports 2021–2023) put built-in apps first: most of the apps used daily are
pre-installed (Safari, Messages, Photos, Mail, Calendar, Notes, Finder), then Office, Chrome and Adobe. The
tasks people automate most on the Mac are image resize/convert, PDF merge and images → PDF, and file
organisation. That gives:

## 35. Do, don't describe: Mac actions in plain English (2026-11-13)

**Report.** "Open the setting app and show bluetooth setting" was answered with how-to text instead of opening the pane.

**Probe.** English action requests run end to end with `ONBUD_DRY_ACTIONS=1`. This new switch reports app, Finder, pane and terminal openings without doing them. Approval actions only propose a command, so nothing ran.

**Why it kept happening.**
1. **Brittle wording rules.** Each skill fires on a hand-written pattern for one wording. Polite forms ("Could you open Notes for me?"), compound requests ("Open Calendar app and show today"), singular nouns ("setting") and other verbs ("pull up", "start Spotify") missed.
2. **Router picks were dropped.** The Decima router often picked the right skill, but the skill's own parser then could not extract the target, so the pick was dropped ("does not apply").
3. **The fallback can only describe.** The last stop is AFM's answer prompt, which cannot act, so it writes instructions. Sometimes it claimed the action was impossible.
4. **Missing actions:** volume up/down, brightness, lock, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth power, Trash, hidden files, quit an app, a folder in Finder. "Make it louder" was even read as the shell command `make`.

**Fix (skills plus one loop step).**
- **`plainRequest`:** strips politeness and padding before the rules. `launchTarget` takes the first clause of a compound request, "get X running", "pop open", and start/run for an app installed under that exact name.
- **Settings:** singular setting/preference and more verbs (see, pull up, get me, I want the …). Distinctive pane names work without the word "settings" (Login Items, Wallpaper, VPN, …). "check for macOS updates" opens Software Update.
- **New `mac_control` actions, all behind approval:**
  - relative and min/max volume, silence
  - brightness keys
  - lock screen
  - Wi-Fi power (networksetup)
  - Bluetooth power: blueutil if installed, else the Bluetooth pane
  - empty the Trash, flagged "cannot be undone"
  - Finder's ⇧⌘. hidden-files toggle (`defaults write` + `killall` is refused by the gate)
  - quit an app; a quit request for an app that is not installed says so

  Finder folders open from `launch_app`.
- **Step 1f, action picker:**
  - **When it runs:** for an imperative request, or a short request that mentions a Mac noun. Questions and developer work are left out.
  - **What AFM does:** picks one action from a closed enum with a target, and never acts itself.
  - **What code does:** checks the pick (appearance vs brightness; a pane named in the request), writes the canonical request, and runs the skill with its usual checks and approval.
  - **If the action can't be done:** the answer prompt must say so plainly and never claim it was done.
- Document-word matching uses word boundaries ("wallpaper" is not "paper").

# OnBud launcher (`apps/spotlight`)

A small, open-source, Spotlight/Raycast-style launcher for local AFM work. Press **⌥ Space**, ask about the
project, approve or deny commands and edits from the panel. It runs without OpenCode, and its setup
installs only what is missing (apfel, Node.js), from their own projects, after asking. Extras come as **plugins**: a router model (Decima by
default), Codex through OpenCode, web search, LaTeX and translation languages. A **chat widget** shows the
last question and answer on the desktop.

| | |
|---|---|
| UI | SwiftUI + AppKit; floating, non-activating panel; menu-bar item (`LSUIElement`, no Dock icon) |
| Hotkey | Carbon `RegisterEventHotKey`, so no Accessibility permission. ⌥ Space by default; ⌃ Space or ⌘ Space in Settings |
| Backend | the OnBud controller on `127.0.0.1:11435` (`bin/afm-agent-server.ts`), which uses apfel/AFM on 11434 and, for S3, a router model on Ollaya (11436) |
| Build | SwiftPM with the Command Line Tools only (no Xcode project) |

## Panel

- **Top row:** the OnBud logo and the "Ask OnBud" field. While a request runs, the reply area shows
  the controller's live steps ("Searching the folder…", "Writing a commit message…", …). The controller
  produces each answer in one structured generation and sends it in one piece, so the panel writes it
  out word by word (at most ~0.8 s) instead of dropping it in at once.
- **Attachments** (they appear as chips under the field):
  - drop files onto the panel;
  - paperclip menu > *Paste from clipboard* (copied text, or files copied in Finder) or *Choose files…*;
  - select text or files in any app > Services > **Ask OnBud**.

  Files are named in the request relative to the project folder. Files outside it switch a new chat to
  their folder (the same folder rules apply). Text is quoted, up to 4,000 characters.
- **Bottom row:**
  - **Folder:** the project folder (default `~/Desktop`), with the last six folders and *Choose folder…*.
  - **Model:** **AFM Agent** (on-device AFM with local tools) or **AFM + <router>** (needs the Router
    model plugin; "AFM + Decima" with decima:agent). With several router models installed, this menu
    also picks one. It also has the web-search switch.
  - **Chevron (⌘L):** folds the answers into one line ("“…” · N answers folded") and back. The chat
    goes on: follow-ups still see the earlier turns and pending approvals stay. **New chat** (⌘N) is
    different: it ends the chat, so the controller forgets the history and pending approvals, and the
    panel is empty again (nothing left to fold).
  - **Earlier answers fold by themselves:** only the latest answer is open; a "▸ N earlier answers folded"
    line unfolds the others. The panel keeps at most five earlier answers; older ones stay in the saved chat
    (clock menu), and the controller still sees the whole chat.
  - **Paperclip:** attachments, as above.
  - **Clock:** the last chats (re-open one and continue it), *Activity…* and *Clear history*.
- **Quick actions** (shown while the panel is empty) fit the folder:
  - *Compile the paper* (needs the LaTeX plugin) and *Check citations*, when there is a `.tex` file;
  - *Describe the documents*, for PDF, Word, slides or images;
  - *Summarize changes*, *Commit message*, *Recent commits* and *Local jobs*, in git repositories
    (the first two run the controller's local `change_summary` / `commit_message` skills);
  - *Terminal here* (the controller's `open_app` skill, in your terminal app) and *Commands*, always.
- **Opening apps:** "open a terminal here", "open it in my editor" and "<app> 열어줘 / open <app>" run the
  controller's `open_app` / `launch_app` skills. Settings > **Apps OnBud opens** picks the terminal,
  editor and browser (`~/OnBud/config/apps.json`, shared with the controller); OnBud's own Terminal
  windows (setup, plugin installs, sign-ins) use the same terminal.
- **Each answer** is rendered from Markdown: headings, tables as grids, lists, quotes and code blocks. It
  has Copy and Save-as-Markdown buttons.
- **Links in answers are clickable** (see How it works for what opens).
- **Notifications:** if the panel is closed when an answer arrives, a notification is shown (Settings).
- **History** is kept in `~/Library/Application Support/OnBud/history.json` (mode 600, last 50 chats).
  Turning it off in Settings deletes it.
- **Activity window** (menu bar or clock menu) lists:
  - the controller's local jobs (`~/OnBud/runtime/jobs`), with *Continue / Apply / Review with Codex /
    Discard* buttons that send the matching chat command, so the usual yes/no approval follows;
  - its background sessions (`tmux -L onbud`).
- **`onbud://ask?q=<text>&folder=<path>`** opens the panel with the question typed in, for Shortcuts,
  Raycast or scripts. It never sends by itself.

## How it works

- **At launch and each time the panel opens**, it probes 127.0.0.1:11434 (apfel `/health`), 11435
  (controller `/health`) and 11436 (Ollaya `/api/tags`). It also looks for `~/OnBud`, the token
  `~/OnBud/config/apfel.token` and the `dev.onbud.agent` / `dev.onbud.apfel` LaunchAgents.
  - If nothing is installed, the panel shows a setup screen with *Set up OnBud…* (see Distribution).
  - If the controller is down, the panel shows the `launchctl kickstart` line instead.
- **Requests** go to `POST /v1/chat/completions` with the bearer token, `stream: true`, and the panel's project
  folder sent as an OpenCode-style `Working directory:` line. The controller only reads folders inside
  `$HOME`, and never `$HOME` itself. Replies stream into the panel.
- **Settings.** The launcher sends `x-onbud-setting: s2|s3`. With that header, the server runs the request
  like the evaluation settings: S2 = rules only, S3 = + router advise, and both with web search and Codex
  off. Without the header the server behaves as before, so OpenCode is unaffected. S3 is used only if
  the router plugin is on and Ollaya is reachable. With S3 the launcher also sends
  `x-onbud-router-model: <name>` for the router model picked in Settings. The thresholds' digest pin
  still applies, so a model other than the calibrated decima:agent is only logged in shadow. As in the
  evaluation, the router advises only on generic routes; skill routes (documents, edits, commands) stay
  with the rules.
- **Approvals.** The controller keeps its own approve/deny flow. In launcher requests, its final stream
  chunk carries `onbud.awaiting`: `command`, `edit`, `apply`, `web`, `job`, `handoff` or `reveal`. The
  panel turns this into buttons:
  - **Yes / No** (⌘↩ / ⌘⌫) send `yes` / `no` as the next turn, which is exactly what you would type in
    OpenCode.
  - The security gate still applies on the server, and edits go sandbox trial → tests → a separate
    "apply?".
- **Escalations** (too big for AFM) offer three choices:
  - **Send to Codex (OpenCode)**: needs the Codex plugin. See Plugins below.
  - **Try locally on a branch**: the controller's local job engine.
  - **No**.

  The launcher's models never call Codex themselves: a `yes` to the controller's hand-off is refused
  server-side.
- **Links in replies.** Markdown links, bare `https://` URLs and `path/to/file` code spans that name an
  existing file (relative to the chat's folder, `file:line` too) are clickable:
  - web (`http`, `https`, `mailto`) opens in the default browser;
  - files and folders inside the home folder open in their app or Finder; anything that could run code
    (apps, scripts, installers, executables) is only selected in Finder;
  - other schemes and paths outside the home folder are not followed.

  A link whose text differs from its target shows the target after it, since replies can quote document
  text.
- **Project folder guard.** The folder must be inside the home folder. These are refused:
  - the home folder itself;
  - hidden folders (`~/.ssh`, `~/.config`, …);
  - `~/Library`, except iCloud Drive.
- **Loopback only.** Every URL is built as `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`; ATS allows only local networking.

## Plugins

AFM Agent is the core and always on. It includes **pdftext**, OnBud's own PDF-text and Vision-OCR
helper, which uses system frameworks only. `make app` builds pdftext into the app, and Backend >
pdftext > *Install* copies it to `~/OnBud/runtime/bin`, where the controller runs it.

Settings > Plugins lists the extras, each with what it is, its status and an on/off switch. A plugin that
is already installed starts out enabled. **Install…** works like this:
1. It explains what will be downloaded.
2. It opens Terminal with the exact commands.
3. Terminal asks `y/N` before running them.

Nothing installs in the background, and macOS asks for your password itself where needed (MacTeX).

| Plugin | Detected by | Install… runs | Adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Router model** | Ollaya on 127.0.0.1:11436, `~/OnBud/runtime/ollaya` or `~/.ollaya/models`; the models from `/api/tags` | `scripts/decima-setup.sh install && pull && start` | the **AFM + <router>** model (Decima by default; pick any installed model) |
| **Codex via OpenCode** | `/Applications/OpenCode.app` or the `opencode` CLI; ready once the OpenCode config has the codex agent | OpenCode's official installer | **Send to Codex** on escalations, **Review with Codex** for jobs |
| **Web search (SearXNG)** | `~/OnBud/runtime/searxng` (running: 127.0.0.1:8888) | `scripts/searxng-setup.sh install && start` (AGPL, ~150 MB) | approval-gated web search; without SearXNG it falls back to DuckDuckGo Lite, arXiv and Wikipedia. Queries leave the Mac |
| **LaTeX (MacTeX)** | `/Library/TeX/texbin/latexmk` | `brew install --cask mactex-no-gui` (~6 GB), or the download page | compiling papers and fixing LaTeX errors (citation checks and polishing work without it) |
| **Remote server (SSH · Fresh/TTT)** | `fresh` on the Mac (Homebrew, Cargo) and the servers it can name (`~/OnBud/config/servers.json`, `Host` names in `~/.ssh/config`) | `brew install fresh-editor` (GPL-3.0, a separate program), or the project page; TTT is installed on the server by you | the `server` skill: run experiments on your server after approval, job state and logs, and a terminal window on it (Fresh, TTT, a shell, tmux attach, `tail -F`). SSH keys are never read |
| **Translation languages** | the Translation framework (each language ↔ English) and `~/OnBud/runtime/bin/afm-translate` | a **Download…** button per language (macOS's own download sheet), *Build now* for the translator | offline translation of Korean questions into English search words (always used when available; without the pack only that step is skipped) |

With the web plugin on, the launcher sends `x-onbud-web: on`. The server then leaves the controller's
web search on for that request, still behind the controller's own "search for …?" approval.

**Send to Codex**:
- **Desktop app installed (preferred):** the launcher reads OpenCode's local service address and
  password from `~/.local/state/opencode/service.json`, accepting only a 127.0.0.1 address. It creates a
  new session (agent `codex`, the project folder, the request as first prompt) and brings OpenCode
  forward. If the app is not running, it is launched first.
- **CLI only (OpenCode 2):** the TUI has no `--agent` flag, so the launcher starts the session on the
  `codex` agent through the CLI's background service (`opencode service start` if it is not running; same
  `service.json`, loopback only) and Terminal opens `opencode <folder> --session <id>` on it. If the service
  cannot be reached, Terminal runs `opencode run --agent codex '<request>'` once and shows how to continue.
  Every argument is single-quoted, and the temporary `.command` file is deleted on the next hand-off.
- **Either way,** Codex runs with OpenCode's own edit/command approvals and the security-gate plugin.

The **Backend** window (menu bar > Backend…, or Settings) starts with **Routing**: the controller and the
three model tiers it routes between, each with its setting.

| Tier | Model | Change it here |
|---|---|---|
| Local LLM | Apple's on-device model through apfel (127.0.0.1:11434) | fixed; shows the context window and whether the model is available |
| Decision model | the router plugin's model on Ollaya (127.0.0.1:11436) | plugin on/off, which installed model, use it in the panel; warns when it is not the calibrated version |
| Code LLM (S5) | GitHub Copilot's inline completion through its official language server (`~/OnBud/runtime/copilot-ls`) | **Copilot mode**: `balanced` (default: checkable code → Copilot first, Codex if it fails; contest-style code → Copilot only when the bundled difficulty classifier calls it easy) or `saver` (Copilot first for all checkable code; fewer Codex calls, slower, less accurate); writes only the `copilot_mode:` line of `policies/routing.yaml`, which the controller reloads |
| Frontier LLM | two tiers: **Strong** = OpenCode's `codex`, `codex-handoff` and `codex-solve` agents (default GPT-6.1 Sol: hand-offs, Send to Codex, code the cheap tier could not verify); **Cheap** = `codex-solve-cheap` (default GPT-6.1 Terra: the code skill's first escalation, kept only when a check passes) | per tier, any model OpenCode lists for your signed-in providers, and the effort (variant). The agent names say the role, so a new model is one setting, not a rename |

- **Frontier changes go into the global OpenCode config** (Show diff → Apply; a backup is written next to
  it, and the write is refused if the file changed meanwhile). Only those agents' `model` / `variant` lines
  change; comments and everything else stay. Because the controller hands off with `opencode run --agent
  codex-handoff`, OnBud's routing and OpenCode switch together (restart the OpenCode app if it is open).
- **Other providers (Claude, GitHub Copilot, …):** *Add a provider key…* opens Terminal with `opencode auth
  login`. The key stays in OpenCode (`~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json`); OnBud only lists which
  providers are signed in (`opencode auth list`) and their models (`opencode models`).

**GitHub Copilot** (below Routing):
- **Status** from the controller's `services/frontier/copilot-ls.ts status` (signed-in user, or not installed).
- **Sign in…** runs its `signin`: the app shows GitHub's device code (Copy code) and opens
  github.com/login/device when you click **Open GitHub**; you sign in on GitHub yourself. The status is
  checked again when the flow ends (it waits up to 10 minutes).
- **Quota** (read-only): `gh api /copilot_internal/user`. OnBud uses only inline completion, which is
  unlimited and spends no premium requests; no Copilot chat, CLI or agent calls.
- **Use Copilot for code** sets or removes `ONBUD_COPILOT=off` in the controller's LaunchAgent after you
  confirm, and restarts the controller. Re-running setup turns it back on.
- Answers whose route went through Copilot carry a **Copilot** label.

**Router model (Ollaya) and SearXNG run only when you start them.** Backend shows each one's state with
**Start** / **Stop** (the decision card in Routing has Start too). Start runs the plugin's setup script

## OpenCode config link (for the Codex plugin)

Settings > OpenCode config reads the global config (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`, else `opencode.json`;
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is honoured). It does nothing when:

- the config is a **symlink to `opencode/opencode.global.jsonc`**, as on the development Mac, or
- the config already has every entry.

Otherwise, **Show diff** shows a unified diff that adds the missing `provider.*`, `agent.*` and `mcp.*`
entries from the repo's `opencode/opencode.global.jsonc`, plus the providers to `enabled_providers` if
the config restricts them. Keys you already have are never changed, with one exception: the MCP entry v0.1.0
added under its old name is replaced by `mcp.onbud` (the diff shows it).

**Back up and merge** works like this:

- It is enabled only after you have seen the diff.
- It copies the file to `opencode.jsonc.afm-spotlight-backup-<time>`, then writes the merge.
- If the file changed after the diff was shown, it refuses to write.
- Comments in the merged file are not kept; they remain in the backup.

## Distribution

- **What ships.** `make app` bundles the controller (`bin`, `services`, `policies`, `scripts`, `opencode`,
  `skills`, and the helper sources `tools/pdftext`, `tools/pdftool`, `tools/pim`, `tools/translate`) in `Contents/Resources/backend`, with a `.onbud-bundled` version
  marker, plus `LICENSE` and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`. No third-party code or model is bundled.
- **Setup** (*Set up OnBud…* in the panel, *Run setup…* in Backend) opens Terminal. It copies the
  bundled controller to `~/OnBud/adaptive-coding-agent` (never over a git checkout or a folder without
  the marker), then runs `scripts/setup.sh`: Homebrew, `brew install apfel`, `brew install node` (22.6+)
  and the two LaunchAgents, each only if missing and only after a `y`. When the app carries a newer
  controller than the installed copy, Backend offers *Update…*.
- **Node is found at run time** (`scripts/node-run.sh`: `$ONBUD_NODE`, PATH, Homebrew, Volta, fnm,
  nvm), and the OpenCode config uses `{env:HOME}`, so no path is tied to one Mac.
- **`make dmg`** → `build/OnBud-<version>.dmg` (app + Applications link + LICENSE). **`make release`**
  (`scripts/release.sh`) also writes version and sha256 into `Casks/onbud.rb` at the repository root and
  prints the tag, `gh release create` and tap commands. It publishes nothing itself. The repository is its
  own Homebrew tap (`brew tap p-yi/onbud https://github.com/P-YI/OnBud`, then `brew trust --cask
  p-yi/onbud/onbud` on Homebrew 7+); the cask depends on the
  `apfel` and `node` formulae.
- **Gatekeeper.** The app is signed ad hoc, not notarized. On macOS 15 and later, right-click > Open no
  longer bypasses the block: users click **Open Anyway** in System Settings > Privacy & Security after the
  first attempt, or run `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/OnBud.app`. A Developer ID
  signature plus notarization (paid Apple Developer Program, hardened runtime) removes the step; the
  official homebrew/cask repository requires that too, so OnBud ships from its own tap.
- **Requirements.** macOS 26 or later on Apple silicon, with **Apple Intelligence** turned on, because the
  on-device Foundation Model is only there. The app itself is built for macOS 15+, so on older systems
  it starts and shows the setup screen; setup stops with the reason.
- **License.** MIT (repository `LICENSE`).
- The Command Line Tools ship no SwiftUI macro plugins, so the code uses `ObservableObject` instead of
  `@State`/`@Observable` (both are macros in the current SDK). There is also no XCTest, so the smoke tool
  (`Sources/SpotlightSmoke`) takes the place of unit tests.

# Benchmarks (v0.2, 2026-11-08)

Measured on one Mac (Apple silicon, macOS 27.x). Small fixed subsets, so read them as direction, not
significance; models are not deterministic and a rerun moves a score by ±1–2. OnBud checks code only against
examples in the problem text (and its own stress test), never against hidden tests. Codex runs through OpenCode
on a ChatGPT subscription: GPT-6.1 Sol (reasoning medium) and, as the cheap tier, GPT-6.1 Terra. "Cost" prices
the measured tokens at API rates: Sol $2 / $0.10 / $10 per 1M input / cached / output; Terra $1 / $0.05 / $5
(a third-party price list; OpenAI's own page was not checked). On-device work and Copilot's inline completion
cost nothing per call.

## At a glance

The default setup is **OnBud (Copilot + Codex)**, a ladder of three writers, cheapest first: GitHub Copilot
(free), then Codex's cheap tier (Terra), then its strong tier (Sol). Every answer must pass a check before it is
kept (the problem's examples, the stress test, or agreement with Copilot's code), and a failed check moves the
task one rung up. Contest-style code starts at Copilot only when a bundled difficulty classifier calls it easy.
v0.1.0 had no Copilot: code went on-device first, then to Codex.

**What Copilot changed.** Copilot alone is far above the on-device model (53 vs 25) at ~9 s a task. Using it as
the writer cut Codex calls from 68 to 27, at first for 3–4 points: Copilot's code could pass a contest problem's
examples and still be wrong.

**What the code skill added (v0.2.0).**
- *Difficulty classifier* (`skills/code/difficulty.json`, `services/controller/code-difficulty.ts`): on the dev
  logs Copilot solved 80% of easy contest problems and 2-6% of medium and hard ones, so trying it on those only
  cost time. Decima's code-difficulty question did not separate them (AUC 0.42-0.59 over four wordings; it is a
  zero-shot encoder that reads text against criteria, not a solver), nor did the on-device model's 1-5 rating
  (0.65). A logistic regression over hashed words, trained on DeepMind CodeContests ratings (CC BY 4.0; 35 KB of
  weights, <1 ms), scored 0.86 (dev LCB) and 0.92 (old test LCB); 0.81 on "Copilot solved it". Short or
  non-English requests are not scored.
- *Ladder with checks:* Terra's answer is kept when the examples pass, or (no examples) when it agrees with
  Copilot's code on generated inputs; otherwise Sol answers. Unchecked Copilot code is no longer kept on an
  inconclusive stress test when Codex is reachable (two of held-out set 2's losses).
- *Stress test* (`stress_pass`): for contest-style code, Copilot also writes a brute force and random-input
  generators; the candidate must agree on small inputs and finish without crashing or timing out on the worst
  case.
- *Retries are not trusted on the examples they were shown*: a candidate written after a failing example must
  pass the stress test (3 of 5 such candidates had been wrong).
- *Code the test cannot judge goes to Codex* (contest-style only).
- *Code nothing else checks* (no examples, no tests; Decima calls it easy) is compared with a brute force on
  small inputs and goes to Codex when they disagree (wrong code kept unchecked: dev 3 → 1–2 a run, test 1 → 0;
  HumanEval/83 and /84 now go to Codex).
- *One Copilot candidate, no retry,* for contest code when Codex is behind it: retries rarely kept a task local
  and cost ~10 s each (dev: 81, 80 with one candidate against 79 with two).
- *Checked escalation tries the smaller model first:* with runnable examples, Codex is asked with GPT-6.1 Terra;
  Sol answers only when Terra's code fails the examples (dev: cost $0.18 → $0.10, 18 → 15 min). This is in the
  code skill (benchmarks, the `afm_code` MCP tool); a local job that escalates still hands the whole task to
  Codex as before.
- *Approach notes* (`skills/code/patterns.json`, 24 algorithm patterns written for OnBud): the on-device model
  picks up to two and they go above Copilot's code as comments. On the held-out LiveCodeBench split Copilot then
  solved 11–12 problems itself instead of 7, and Codex calls fell from 23 to 18–19 at the same accuracy.
- Cost of the gate: ~6 extra Copilot requests (~10 s) on contest-style tasks only; nothing on others.
- Tried and not shipped (held-out LiveCodeBench): asking Codex for a plan first and letting Copilot write it
  (Codex calls 23 → 42, cost +70%); a private notebook of earlier Codex solutions (no fewer calls); a brute force
  written by the on-device model; a cue-based tagger for the notes. Details: `docs/skills-plan.md` §25–27.

# How OnBud works (v0.2)

OnBud puts Apple's on-device Foundation Model to work on your own files, with code doing everything the
small model is bad at: finding files, reading documents, running and checking things, and asking you before
anything changes. Larger tasks can be handed to Codex through OpenCode, if you turn that on.

```text
 ⌥ Space ─► OnBud.app (SwiftUI launcher, widget, menu bar)
                │  http://127.0.0.1:11435  (bearer token, loopback only)
                ▼
          OnBud controller (Node, bin/afm-agent-server.ts)
          ├─ security gate · secret redaction · project-folder guard
          ├─ router (rules, optional local router model) ─► local skill / AFM / Codex hand-off
          ├─ context builder: Spotlight + ripgrep search, PDF/Office/iWork/HWPX/image reading (OCR), sheets
          ├─ tools: commands (approval), edits (sandbox trial + tests, then approval), LaTeX, web (approval)
          └─ memory, telemetry, local jobs in git worktrees
                │  http://127.0.0.1:11434
                ▼
          apfel ─► Apple FoundationModels (on-device)        optional: Ollaya + Decima (11436),
                                                             SearXNG (8888), OpenCode + Codex,
                                                             GitHub Copilot (language server)
```

## What is implemented

**Launcher app** (`apps/spotlight`, Swift, built with the Command Line Tools only)
- Floating panel on a global hotkey (⌥ Space; ⌃ Space or ⌘ Space in Settings), project-folder and model
  menus, quick actions that fit the folder (papers, documents, git changes, commit messages).
- Answers rendered from Markdown (headings, tables, lists, code) and written out progressively, with live
  progress steps from the controller; clickable links (web pages, files in your home folder).
- Approve / deny buttons for every command, edit, web search and local job; fold the answers or start a
  new chat; history, attachments (drop files, clipboard, Services menu "Ask OnBud"), `onbud://` URLs.
- Chat widget (WidgetKit), menu-bar logo that lights up while the model works, notifications.
- Guided setup and plugins: each extra is installed from its own project, in Terminal, after asking.

**Controller** (`bin/`, `services/`, `policies/`, Node 22.6+, no npm dependencies)
- **Routing:** deterministic rules decide between a local skill, the on-device model, asking you, or a
  Codex hand-off; an optional router model (Decima on Ollaya) can advise on generic requests.
- **Skills** (`skills/<id>/skill.json`, 13 packs): each declares what it may do (read, propose, run approved,
  write new files, network, frontier, remote), what leaves the Mac, and the checks that make an answer green; a switch
  per skill in the Skills window (`config/skills.json`); a skill eval gates changes. For requests no rule
  claims, the on-device model picks a skill from its example requests, or none. Replies follow the request's
  language (nine languages), with code, paths, numbers and names kept exactly.
- **Code** (`services/controller/code-skill.ts`): a ladder of writers, cheapest first: Copilot's inline
  completion (free), Codex's cheap tier (default Terra), its strong tier (default Sol; both models are picked in
  Backend > Routing). The on-device model plans and checks
  (examples, the project's tests, a stress test against a brute force, agreement between two writers on
  generated inputs); a failed check moves the task one rung up. Contest-style code starts at Copilot only when
  a bundled difficulty classifier (`code-difficulty.ts`) calls it easy. Who writes first is one rule
  (`firstWriter`) for local jobs and the benchmark; `copilot_mode` in `policies/routing.yaml` (`balanced` by
  default, the measured setup; `saver` tries Copilot first on all checkable code).
- **Remote servers** (`services/server`, skill `server`): the project is uploaded (secrets and big files left out)
  and a command started on the user's server after approval, over the system `ssh` (keys never read); job state
  and logs come back on request, and a terminal window shows the server (Fresh on the Mac, or TTT, a shell, the
  job's tmux session or its log there). The code is still written on the Mac, so the ladder applies.
- **Mac tasks:** file conversion, Shortcuts, appearance / volume / screenshot (on approval), the front browser
  tab, calendar and reminders (read-only, off by default).
- **Work graphs and strategy memory:** independent steps run together with at most three attempts each; plans
  and their verdicts are remembered per skill and recalled for similar requests.
- **Local skills** (code gathers and checks, the model fills small schemas): commit messages, change
  summaries, release notes, error-log triage, translation, docstrings, privacy scan, CSV ↔ JSON,
  spreadsheet lookup, slide outlines, git and GitHub (read-only) status, Mac health check.
- **Documents:** PDF text and Vision OCR (`tools/pdftext`), Word, slides, spreadsheets, iWork, HWPX and
  images; questions are framed, the whole document is searched, and answers are checked against the lines
  they cite.
- **Commands and edits:** read-only commands run directly; anything else waits for approval. Edits are
  tried in a sandbox copy with the project's tests before a separate "apply?" question. Long runs go to
  background sessions (tmux).
- **Local jobs:** offline multi-step code or LaTeX work in a git worktree, with a journal, then
  Continue / Apply / Review / Discard.
- **LaTeX:** compile with latexmk, summarize the log, fix errors, check citations and references.
- **Web search** (off unless enabled): every query needs your approval; local SearXNG if installed.
- **Safety:** a security gate shared by the controller and both OpenCode engines (destructive commands,
  secrets, paths outside the project), secret redaction before any model call, loopback-only services.
- **OpenCode integration:** the controller doubles as the `afm` agent and an MCP server
  (`bin/afm-mcp-server.ts`) that gives frontier agents local document, search and LaTeX tools.

## Design references

OnBud reimplemented ideas from these projects (no code was copied); see `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`.
- **apfel:** the on-device model behind an OpenAI-compatible API.
- **fm-guide:** document chunks of about 1.5k tokens; "structure, never truth", hence the check that cited
  paths exist; temperature 0.
- **fm-proxy:** one-schema tool dispatch (forced calls as one object with a property per tool); guardrail
  refusals as their own failure class; retries only for transient errors; output caps.
- **LocalCode:** the model proposes shell commands, the user approves them.
- **OpenClaw (`apple-fm`):** the on-device model is a utility model; the host owns tool execution and approvals.
- **me-box:** one git worktree per concurrent task, durable sessions, a running record of the build state.
- **Laya / Ollaya / Decima:** typed routing decisions (route, secret, destructive) from a small local model.

## Limits

- The on-device model has an 8,192-token window (4,096 on older Macs and macOS 26); long documents are
  searched and excerpted, never read whole.
- On its own it solves few coding benchmark problems (see `BENCHMARKS.md`): code is written by Copilot when
  the plugin is on; multi-file changes, new features and hard debugging are what the Codex hand-off is for.
- The stress test cannot catch an error the brute force shares (both written by Copilot), and it judges
  contest-style code only; other code is checked by its examples and the project's tests.
- OnBud does not use Apple's `fm` command-line tool or Private Cloud Compute (see the README).

| `raw` | The on-device model alone (Apple Foundation Model via apfel), one schema-constrained answer. Question tasks only. |
| `s2` | AFM with the controller's local tools: files, documents, terminal with approval, edits checked in a sandbox, local jobs, LaTeX, local skills. No Decima, no web, no frontier. |
| `s3` | S2 plus the Decima router (321M, Ollaya on 127.0.0.1:11436) in advise mode. |
| `s1` | S3 plus approval-gated web search (SearXNG) and Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol through OpenCode) as a fallback. |
| `codex` | Codex alone, through OpenCode, one attempt per task. |
| `copilot` | Code only: GitHub Copilot's inline completion writes, checked on-device, no Codex. |
| `s5` | Code only: Copilot writes, the code skill's checks (examples, tests, stress test), Codex for what fails. The v0.2.0 default. |

## Suites

### 1. Task suite (`framework-eval.ts`): the framework's own work

The suite has 66 tasks per run in 15 categories (A or P, plus C to K, Q, R, V and X). Each task builds a fresh fixture: a small git repository (with a remote and a worktree for R), a LaTeX paper, generated documents, or generated spreadsheets and slides. It then sends one request and checks the result in code, from the files or the answer text.

| Category | Tasks | What is checked |
|---|---|---|
| A docs (private) | 5 | Facts from the author's own PDF archive. **Not public:** `--public` replaces this category with P. |
| P docs (public) | 5 | Facts from generated PDF, DOCX and text files (sender, venue, totals, benchmark name, dates). |
| C terminal | 6 | Counting files and lines, the git branch, recent commits, the largest file, where a function is defined. |
| D edit+tests | 2 | Bug fixes that must make the repository's tests pass. |
| E jobs | 3 | Multi-step changes: a new function plus a new test file, a project-wide rename, a new module. |
| F LaTeX | 3 | Compile and fix, missing citations and references, a new section inserted in the right place. |
| G web | 3 | Facts that need a web search (S1 only; deferred in S2/S3). |
| H chat | 1 | Plain question. |
| I safety | 4 | `rm -rf` and `curl \| sh` are not run, `.env` is not revealed, a prompt injection inside a file is ignored. |
| J dev assist | 4 | Commit message from the staged diff, summary of uncommitted changes, release notes, cause of a logged traceback. |
| K text tools | 5 | Action-item table, translation, docstrings (code unchanged, by AST), privacy scan, CSV→JSON. |
| R repo state | 3 | Branch ahead of and behind its remote (with the commits on each side), a worktree with uncommitted work, what to do before pushing. Local git only: the remote is a bare repository next to the fixture. |
| V docs (held out) | 10 | Other facts of the P documents in other phrasings (due date, who is billed, authors, a count, the letter's purpose and recipient, a line item, the last page, the venue in English and colloquial Korean). Written before their first run; used to check that changes to the document path generalise beyond P. |
| X office | 8 | A workbook with group heading rows (the heading in one column, the rows below belonging to it), a vertically merged column and two sheets; a deck whose slide files are stored out of presentation order, with a table and speaker notes. Files sit in folders named with spaces, Hangul and brackets. Checks: every supplier across two matching groups, a price, the rows of a merged cell, a name not in the sheet, an English question, slide titles in order, a table cell, a note. |
| Q reworded | 9 | The J/K requests in other words, with the same checks. They test that skill detection is not tied to one phrasing. Two of the nine were missed on their first run, and the patterns were widened afterwards, so Q is no longer held out. |

A task passes only if its check passes. A task that needs web or Codex in a setting that has neither is counted as **deferred**, not failed.

### 2. Code benchmarks (`code-eval.ts`): algorithmic coding

| Subset | Problems | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `humaneval-40` | 40 | HumanEval (MIT) |
| `lcb-v6-30` | 30 (10 easy, 10 medium, 10 hard) | LiveCodeBench code_generation_lite v6 |
| `bcb-hard-stdlib` | 25 | BigCodeBench-Hard v0.1.4, stdlib-only tasks |
| `ml` / `mlh` | 15 / 6 | The repository's own ML implementation tasks (regression, ridge, gradient descent, logistic regression, k-means, kNN, naive Bayes, PCA, TF-IDF, word2vec pairs, an SGNS update, nearest words, metrics, softmax; held out: z-score, covariance, R², polynomial fit, word analogy, k-fold). Pure Python, numeric checks; built and checked by `make-ml-impl.py`. |
| `dev-*` | 30 / 30 / 25 | Disjoint dev splits for tuning (`make-dev-subsets.ts` refuses any overlap) |

- **Protocol:** greedy pass@1 against the hidden tests. Generated code runs under `sandbox-exec`, with no outside network and writes only in temp directories.
- **Tuning rule:** any setting is tuned on `dev-*` only. Each test subset is run once per version, and reuse is reported.
- **Data:** the datasets are downloaded by `fetch-code-benchmarks.sh` and are not redistributed here.

### 3. Skill eval (`tools/skill-eval.ts`)

The public cases in `skills/<id>/evals/cases.jsonl` (request, folder, programmatic checks), run three times
each and scored by majority: `npm run skills:eval -- --repeat 3`. Cases about real documents live in
`~/OnBud/runtime/evals/private` and are never committed.

## Run

```sh
tools/bench/run-suite.sh --public                  # task suite, s2 s3 s1 (+ codex if OpenCode is set up), then the report
tools/bench/run-suite.sh --public --code           # also the code benchmarks (downloads the datasets first)
tools/bench/run-suite.sh --settings s2             # one setting; --public leaves out the private archive tasks
tools/bench/cleanup-local.sh                       # delete datasets, fixtures and bench jobs; results and logs stay
```

Requirements:
- macOS 26 or later with Apple Intelligence on, and apfel serving AFM on 11434 (`scripts/` in this repository).
- Node 22, and Python 3.11 or later (uv) for scoring.
- Optional, each for one setting or category:
  - Ollaya with `decima:agent` (S3)
  - a TeX distribution (F)
  - SearXNG on 8888 (G)
  - OpenCode with the `codex-handoff` and `codex-solve` agents (S1, `codex`)
- `/usr/bin/zip` for the X fixtures (built from `office-fixtures.ts`; no third-party files)

## Report

`report-eval.ts` merges every result into `docs/benchmark-results-<date>.md`. The report has these tables:
- the task suite by category and setting, with latency, Codex calls and web searches;
- the code benchmarks, by version and with the S1 route breakdown;
- speed and cost.

Codex cost is API-equivalent, from tokens measured per call (`ctok` in each result line). Codex runs on a subscription, so nothing is billed per token. Publish the report together with the `results-*.jsonl` files and `logs/`.

## What to report with a result

- Mac model and memory, macOS version, apfel version, and the Decima digest (`policies/routing.yaml`).
- Any task that did not run, and why: no TeX, no web, no Codex.
- For code benchmarks: which version and settings were used, and how many times the test subsets had already been used.
